pages.activity_name: Infantry field work and foot patrols
pages.summary: Day-to-day grunt work: dismounted patrols, humping gear in body armor, and living out of a pack for weeks on deployment or in training.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral or cervical strain
common_conditions.reason: Hours in body armor, heavy gear and walking patrols strain the low back muscles and joints.

common_conditions.name: Meniscus, Dislocated (Locking, Pain, Effusion)
common_conditions.reason: Loaded pivots, kneeling and rough ground tear knee cartilage; infantry show more meniscus tears.

common_conditions.name: Ankle, limited motion of
common_conditions.reason: Patrolling uneven ground under load rolls ankles; infantry have more ankle sprains than most jobs.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Weapons fire and blasts around combat jobs damage the inner ear and cause ringing.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Repeated gunfire near the ear wears down hearing; combat arms Marines show worse thresholds.

common_conditions.name: Intervertebral Disc Syndrome (Herniated Disc)
common_conditions.reason: Heavy armor and carry loads compress the lower discs and can push them out of place.

common_conditions.name: Degenerative arthritis, other than post-traumatic
common_conditions.reason: Service members get arthritis more than civilians their age, most often in the knee and shoulder.

common_conditions.name: Metatarsalgia, anterior (Morton's disease), unilateral, or bilateral
common_conditions.reason: Long loaded marches pound the forefoot and inflame the nerves between the toes.

common_conditions.name: Paralysis of external cutaneous nerve of the thigh
common_conditions.reason: Hip belts and body armor press on the thigh's outer skin nerve and cause burning numbness.

common_conditions.name: Hernia (Inguinal, Femoral, Umbilical, Ventral, Incisional)
common_conditions.reason: Heavy lifting and loaded carries raise belly pressure; combat jobs show more groin hernias.

common_conditions.name: Tibia and fibula, impairment of
common_conditions.reason: Repeated foot strikes under load can crack the tibia or fibula as a stress fracture.

common_conditions.name: Foot injuries, other
common_conditions.reason: Long marches under load cause metatarsal stress fractures and lasting foot injury.

common_conditions.name: Metatarsalgia, anterior (Morton's disease), unilateral, or bilateral
common_conditions.reason: Load pressing through the forefoot on long marches causes metatarsalgia.

common_conditions.name: Paralysis of upper radicular group (5th and 6th cervicals)
common_conditions.reason: Rucksack straps press on the brachial plexus and can cause rucksack palsy in the arm.

common_conditions.name: Paralysis of external cutaneous nerve of the thigh
common_conditions.reason: Hip belts press on the outer thigh nerve and cause numb, burning thighs (meralgia paresthetica).

common_conditions.name: Paralysis of long thoracic nerve
common_conditions.reason: Ruck straps can compress the long thoracic nerve and cause shoulder blade weakness.

sources.title: Injuries associated with strenuous road marching.
sources.supports: In a 20 km, 46 kg road march, 24% of infantry soldiers were injured; all injuries hit the legs or back.

sources.title: Soldier load carriage: historical, physiological, biomechanical, and medical aspects.
sources.supports: Army review listing common load carriage injuries: stress fractures, back strains, metatarsalgia, rucksack palsy and knee pain.

sources.title: Soldier occupational load carriage: a narrative review of associated injuries.
sources.supports: Load carriage injuries center on the lower limbs: stress fractures, knee and foot pain, neuropathies, back injuries and rucksack palsy.
sources.publisher: Int J Inj Contr Saf Promot

sources.title: Risk factors for injury associated with low, moderate, and high mileage road marching in a U.S. Army infantry brigade.
sources.supports: APHC study: road marching injury risk rises with load over 25% of body weight and with more pound-miles per month.

sources.title: Load Carriage-Related Paresthesias: Part 1: Rucksack Palsy and Digitalgia Paresthetica.
sources.supports: Rucksack palsy is a traction or compression injury of the brachial plexus caused by rucksack shoulder straps.

sources.title: Load Carriage-Related Paresthesias (Part 2): Meralgia Paresthetica.
sources.supports: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) is reported from hip belts, pistol belts, parachute harnesses and body armor.

sources.title: Isolated Mononeuropathy From Rucksack Palsy: A Case Series.
sources.supports: Walter Reed case series of rucksack-related long thoracic and spinal accessory nerve injuries.

pages.summary: Static line and military freefall (HALO/HAHO) jumps, including opening shock, night and combat-load jumps, and parachute landing falls.

common_conditions.name: Ankle, limited motion of
common_conditions.reason: The ankle takes the most parachute landing injuries, sprains and fractures.

common_conditions.name: Residuals of traumatic brain injury (TBI)
common_conditions.reason: Head strikes on landing cause closed head injuries, about 3 per 1,000 jumps.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Hard landings and opening shock strain the back; back strains rank among top jump injuries.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Parachute opening shock and landings jolt the neck under helmet weight and strain it.

common_conditions.name: Knee, other impairment of
common_conditions.reason: Hard or twisting landings can tear knee ligaments.

common_conditions.name: Tibia and fibula, impairment of
common_conditions.reason: Landing forces can fracture the lower leg; fractures lead freefall training injuries.

common_conditions.name: Intervertebral Disc Syndrome (Herniated Disc)
common_conditions.reason: Sudden neck flexion at canopy opening has been linked to cervical disc protrusion.

common_conditions.name: Paralysis of external cutaneous nerve of the thigh
common_conditions.reason: Parachute harness straps can compress the outer thigh nerve (meralgia paresthetica).

common_conditions.name: Degenerative arthritis, other than post-traumatic
common_conditions.reason: Veteran military parachutists show higher rates of knee and hip arthritis.

sources.title: Injuries in military parachuting: a prospective study of 4499 jumps.
sources.supports: The ankle was the most injured site and 80% of jump injuries hit the legs; severe ones included fractures and knee ligament tears.

sources.title: Risk Factors for Injuries During Military Static-Line Airborne Operations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.supports: APHC meta-analysis: night jumps, combat loads, high winds and skipping the parachute ankle brace raise jump injury risk.

sources.title: Risk factors for closed-head injuries during military airborne operations.
sources.supports: In 96,132 jumps there were 310 closed-head injuries; 98% came on landing.

sources.title: Parachuting injury surveillance, Fort Bragg, North Carolina, May 1993 to December 1994.
sources.supports: At Fort Bragg, leg injuries, back and neck strains and closed head injuries were the leading jump injuries.

sources.title: Military free fall training injuries.
sources.supports: HALO training injuries were mostly fractures and sprains, hitting the legs, arms and spine, mainly on landing.

sources.title: Cervical Spine Injuries and Head-Supported Mass: A Descriptive Epidemiology Study in Special Operations Combat Soldiers.
sources.supports: Special operators reported neck sprains and strains from whiplash, parachute opening shock and landings while wearing helmets.

sources.title: Military parachuting injuries: a literature review.
sources.supports: Occupational medicine review of static line parachuting injury mechanisms and classic parachuting injuries.

sources.title: Neck injury after repeated flexions due to parachuting.
sources.supports: Case: HALO canopy opening led to C7 root damage with cervical disc protrusions and degeneration.

sources.title: Load Carriage-Related Paresthesias (Part 2): Meralgia Paresthetica.
sources.supports: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) is reported from hip belts, pistol belts, parachute harnesses and body armor.

sources.title: Osteoarthritis and the Tactical Athlete: A Systematic Review.
sources.supports: Service members and veteran parachutists had higher rates of knee, hip or any osteoarthritis than unexposed groups.

pages.summary: Initial entry training: sudden jumps in running, marching, drill and field training for weeks, often in heat, before the body adapts.

common_conditions.name: Tibia and fibula, impairment of
common_conditions.reason: A sudden jump in running and marching cracks the tibia; recruit stress fracture rates are high.

common_conditions.name: Shin Splints (Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome)
common_conditions.reason: Shin splints affect 35% to 56% of recruits as training loads ramp up fast.

common_conditions.name: Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (PFPS)
common_conditions.reason: The knee is the most injured site in basic training, much of it overuse kneecap pain.

common_conditions.name: Foot injuries, other
common_conditions.reason: Metatarsal stress fractures are among the most common recruit foot injuries.

common_conditions.name: Femur, impairment of
common_conditions.reason: Femoral neck stress fractures in trainees can need surgery and end service.

common_conditions.name: Ankle, limited motion of
common_conditions.reason: Ankle sprains are a leading recruit injury, and prior sprains raise injury risk.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: The low back is the second most injured area in initial entry training.

common_conditions.name: Heat Injury Residuals (Heat Stroke / Heat Exhaustion)
common_conditions.reason: Unacclimated recruits training in hot months suffer heat illness, mostly in the first weeks.

common_conditions.name: Rhabdomyolysis, residuals of
common_conditions.reason: Recruits have the highest exertional rhabdomyolysis rates, from extreme muscle breakdown.

sources.title: Incidence and Risk Factors for the Development of Stress Fractures in Military Recruits and Qualified Personnel: A Systematic Review.
sources.supports: Review of 70 studies: stress fractures hit the tibia, fibula and metatarsals most, far more often in recruits.
sources.publisher: Int J Environ Res Public Health

sources.title: Stress Fractures: Etiology, Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Prevention.
sources.supports: Stress fractures come from repeated loading; Army basic trainees run 19 (men) and 80 (women) per 1,000.

sources.title: Highlights of Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome in Military Recruits: A Narrative Review.
sources.supports: Review of 35 studies: shin splints (MTSS) affect 35% to 56% of military recruits, driven by training demands.

sources.title: Gait retraining and incidence of medial tibial stress syndrome in army recruits.
sources.supports: British Army trial tracked medial tibial stress syndrome in 450 recruits over 26 weeks of basic training.

sources.title: The Etiology of Injuries in US Army Initial Entry Training.
sources.supports: APHC: in 106,367 trainees, 75% of injuries hit the legs, mostly overuse; the knee was the top site, then the low back.

sources.title: Epidemiology of injuries associated with physical training among young men in the army.
sources.supports: In infantry basic training, 37% had leg injuries; strains, sprains and overuse knee problems led, with high running mileage a risk.

sources.title: Surgically Treated Femoral Neck Stress Fractures Are Likely to Result in Military Separation During Basic Combat Training.
sources.supports: Femoral neck stress fractures are common in basic combat trainees and often end in surgery and separation.

sources.title: Incidence, timing, and seasonal patterns of heat illnesses during U.S. Army basic combat training, 2014-2018.
sources.supports: 1,210 heat illness events in Army basic training from 2014 to 2018, over half in the first 3 weeks.

sources.title: Exertional rhabdomyolysis among active component members of the U.S. Armed Forces, 2020-2024.
sources.supports: Recruit trainees had the highest exertional rhabdomyolysis rates, over 13 times those of other members.

pages.summary: Hours a day in plate carriers, IOTV or flak vests and helmets with NVGs on patrol, guard, convoys or standby.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: More hours in body armor each day predicted low back pain on deployment.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Armor and helmet mass load the neck; neck pain rises with 4 or more hours a day in armor.

common_conditions.name: Arm, limitation of motion of
common_conditions.reason: Plate weight hangs on the shoulders; shoulder visits rose when armor was mandated.

common_conditions.name: Paralysis of external cutaneous nerve of the thigh
common_conditions.reason: Armor and belts press on the outer thigh nerve, causing numb, burning thighs.

common_conditions.name: Intervertebral Disc Syndrome (Herniated Disc)
common_conditions.reason: Years of heavy armor and loads are linked to early low back disc herniation in veterans.

common_conditions.name: Neuralgia of sciatic nerve (sciatica)
common_conditions.reason: Disc herniation after armor wear often brings sciatic leg pain.

sources.title: Loads worn by soldiers predict episodes of low back pain during deployment to Afghanistan.
sources.supports: In 805 deployed soldiers, more hours in body armor and heavier gear predicted low back pain.

sources.title: A comparison of deployed occupational tasks performed by different types of military battalions and resulting low back pain.
sources.supports: Time in body armor and prior back pain were the most consistent predictors of low back pain on deployment.

sources.title: Association between back, neck, and upper extremity musculoskeletal pain and the individual body armor.
sources.supports: Survey of 863 soldiers in Iraq: back, neck and arm pain rose on deployment and tracked with 4+ hours a day in armor.

sources.title: Cervical Spine Injuries and Head-Supported Mass: A Descriptive Epidemiology Study in Special Operations Combat Soldiers.
sources.supports: Special operators reported neck sprains and strains from whiplash, parachute opening shock and landings while wearing helmets.

sources.title: Injuries Associated With Mandated Wear of Body Armor in Iraq.
sources.supports: When body armor was mandated, musculoskeletal visits rose, led by shoulder and back, with more neck injuries.

sources.title: Meralgia paresthetica due to body armor wear in U.S. soldiers serving in Iraq: a case report and review of the literature.
sources.supports: Two soldiers in Iraq developed meralgia paresthetica most likely from repetitive body armor wear.

sources.title: Load Carriage-Related Paresthesias (Part 2): Meralgia Paresthetica.
sources.supports: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) is reported from hip belts, pistol belts, parachute harnesses and body armor.

sources.title: Body Armor and Lumbar Disc Herniation in Young Military Veterans: A Case Series.
sources.supports: VA case series: young veterans with L4-S1 disc herniation and radicular pain after heavy armor and load wear.

pages.summary: Long hours in Humvees, MRAPs, Strykers and LMTVs over rough roads in armor, with jolts, vibration and turret time.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Hours of jolting and vibration in a seat, under armor and gear, wear out the low back.

common_conditions.name: Neuralgia of sciatic nerve (sciatica)
common_conditions.reason: Whole-body vibration from vehicle rides is tied to sciatic nerve pain down the leg.

common_conditions.name: Intervertebral Disc Syndrome (Herniated Disc)
common_conditions.reason: Long-term vibration exposure raises the risk of a herniated lumbar disc.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Jolts and bouncing with a helmet on load the neck in ground vehicles.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Engine, road and track noise inside military vehicles can exceed safe limits for hours.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Long rides in loud vehicles add to the noise that causes ringing in the ears.

sources.title: Loads worn by soldiers predict episodes of low back pain during deployment to Afghanistan.
sources.supports: In a deployed Army brigade, 21 to 40 hours a week in a tactical vehicle, body armor time and load weight raised low back pain risk.

sources.title: Vehicle Exposure and Spinal Musculature Fatigue in Military Warfighters: A Meta-Analysis.
sources.supports: Meta-analysis: military vehicle rides significantly fatigued the lumbar muscles.

sources.title: Whole-body vibration and the risk of low back pain and sciatica: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.supports: Meta-analysis of 20 studies: whole-body vibration roughly doubled the odds of low back pain (OR 2.17) and sciatica (OR 1.92).

sources.title: Exposure to whole-body vibration and hospitalization due to lumbar disc herniation.
sources.supports: Cohort of 288,926 workers: medium to high whole-body vibration raised hospitalization for lumbar disc herniation (RR 1.35).

sources.title: Effects of vehicle-ride exposure on cervical pathology: a meta-analysis.
sources.supports: Meta-analysis: ground vehicle rides (OR 2.33) and fixed-wing flight, especially fighter jets (OR 1.78), raised cervical pathology.

sources.title: In-vehicle noise exposure among military personnel depending on type of vehicle, riding compartment and road surface.
sources.supports: Noise inside armored personnel carriers and military trucks exceeded limits, putting riders at high risk of noise-induced hearing loss.

sources.title: Noise and Military Service: Implications for Hearing Loss and Tinnitus
sources.supports: National Academies review of hazardous military noise and the noise levels that cause hearing loss and tinnitus.
sources.publisher: Institute of Medicine, The National Academies Press

pages.summary: Pilot, crew chief, gunner or medic time in helicopters: rotor vibration, bent posture, heavy helmets with NVGs and engine noise.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Rotor vibration and hours bent forward in the seat wear on the low back.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Heavy helmets with night vision goggles strain the neck on every flight.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Rotor and engine noise damages hearing over a flying career.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Helicopter pilots are diagnosed with tinnitus at about 3 times the rate of ground crews.

common_conditions.name: Arm, limitation of motion of
common_conditions.reason: Shoulder pain is common in helicopter crews from posture and controls.

sources.title: Prevalence of Back and Neck Complaints in Military Rotary Wing Aircrew: A Systematic Review.
sources.supports: Review of 28 studies (3,786 military helicopter aircrew): pooled back pain 64% and neck pain 52%.

sources.title: Reported Back Pain in Army Aircrew in Relation to Airframe, Gender, Age, and Experience.
sources.supports: 84.6% of 467 U.S. Army aviation crewmembers reported back pain during their flying career.

sources.title: Prevalence and potential risk factors of flight-related neck, shoulder and low back pain among helicopter pilots and crewmembers: a questionnaire-based study.
sources.supports: Helicopter pilots: 67% neck, 48% low back, 43% shoulder pain in 12 months; night vision goggle use nearly doubled neck pain odds.

sources.title: Army and Marine Aviation Corps Exposome Signatures From the Pharmaceutical Impacts on Tinnitus and Hearing Loss.
sources.supports: Army and Marine helicopter pilots had almost 3 times the tinnitus rate and twice the hearing loss rate of ground crew controls.

sources.title: Hearing in military pilots: one-time audiometry in pilots of fighters, transports, and helicopters.
sources.supports: 521 military pilots: noise notch at 6 kHz; fighter and helicopter pilots had higher hearing loss risk than transport pilots.

pages.summary: Launching, recovering, fueling, loading and fixing aircraft on the flight line: jet noise, fuels, solvents and awkward postures.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Jet engine noise plus fuel and solvent exposure damages hearing in maintainers.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Flight support crews report ringing ears tied to noise-related hearing loss.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Lifting, bending and reaching into aircraft at awkward angles strains the low back.

common_conditions.name: Arm, limitation of motion of
common_conditions.reason: Overhead work and heavy parts lead to shoulder disorders in aircraft maintainers.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Looking up into wheel wells and panels for hours strains the neck.

sources.title: Effect of noise and ototoxicants on developing standard threshold shifts at a U.S. Air Force depot level maintenance facility.
sources.supports: 2,372 USAF aircraft maintainers: metal plus solvent exposure with noise raised hearing threshold shift risk (RR 2.44).

sources.title: Noise and Military Service: Implications for Hearing Loss and Tinnitus
sources.supports: National Academies review of hazardous military noise and the noise levels that cause hearing loss and tinnitus.
sources.publisher: Institute of Medicine, The National Academies Press

sources.title: [A cross-sectional study and risk factors analysis of tinnitus in flight support personnel of PLA air force].
sources.supports: 24.2% of 666 air force flight support personnel had tinnitus, tied to high-frequency hearing loss.
sources.publisher: Lin Chuang Er Bi Yan Hou Tou Jing Wai Ke Za Zhi

sources.title: Serum lipids and low back pain in male aircraft maintenance technicians: association after ergonomic exposure adjustment.
sources.supports: 42.4% of 1,713 aircraft maintenance technicians had low back pain; high back exposure and work pace raised the odds.

sources.title: Musculoskeletal disorders and psychosocial risk factors among workers of the aircraft maintenance industry.
sources.supports: Aircraft maintenance workers: low back most affected; exams found shoulder disorders; neck also painful.

pages.summary: Launch and recovery crews on aircraft carriers and big-deck amphibs: jet blast noise, 12-hour days, steel decks and chains.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Flight deck noise averages 109 dBA over 11-hour days, causing hearing loss.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Constant jet noise with little quiet time to recover leads to ringing in the ears.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Hauling chains, chocks and gear on steel decks makes low back injury the top complaint.

common_conditions.name: Knee, other impairment of
common_conditions.reason: Kneeling on steel decks and slips around moving aircraft injure the knees.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Neck injuries on the flight deck cost sailors lost duty time.

sources.title: Hearing health risk in a population of aircraft carrier flight deck personnel.
sources.supports: Carrier flight deck crews averaged 109 dBA over 11.5-hour days; 17% of flight deck and 27% of engineers had hearing loss vs 4%.

sources.title: Living at Work: 24-hour Noise Exposure Aboard US Navy Aircraft Carriers.
sources.supports: On a Nimitz-class carrier, 93% of sailors exceeded the 24-hour noise limit, with little quiet time for ears to recover.

sources.title: Noise and Military Service: Implications for Hearing Loss and Tinnitus
sources.supports: National Academies review of hazardous military noise and the noise levels that cause hearing loss and tinnitus.
sources.publisher: Institute of Medicine, The National Academies Press

sources.title: Incidence and Mechanisms of Musculoskeletal Injuries in Deployed Navy Active Duty Service Members Aboard Two U.S. Navy Air Craft Carriers.
sources.supports: On two deployed carriers, low back (34%), shoulder (25%) and knee (15%) were the most common musculoskeletal complaints.

sources.title: At work and play in a hazardous environment: injuries aboard a deployed U.S. Navy aircraft carrier.
sources.supports: 335 injuries on a deployed carrier's flight deck, hangar bay and gym; lower extremity, neck and back injuries cost the most duty time.

pages.summary: Living and working aboard ship: steep ladder wells, hatches, steel decks, heavy lifting, and loud engine rooms and machinery spaces.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Lifting, climbing ladders and working in tight spaces make low back injury the top complaint.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Engine rooms are the loudest spaces aboard, and engineers show high hearing loss rates.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Engine and machinery noise at sea is tied to ringing in the ears.

common_conditions.name: Arm, limitation of motion of
common_conditions.reason: Shoulder injuries are the second most common sailor complaint on deployed ships.

common_conditions.name: Knee, other impairment of
common_conditions.reason: Ladders, hatches and knee knockers make knee injuries common aboard ship.

sources.title: Incidence and Mechanisms of Musculoskeletal Injuries in Deployed Navy Active Duty Service Members Aboard Two U.S. Navy Air Craft Carriers.
sources.supports: On two deployed carriers, low back (34%), shoulder (25%) and knee (15%) were the most common musculoskeletal complaints.

sources.title: Epidemiology of musculoskeletal and soft tissue injuries aboard a U.S. Navy ship.
sources.supports: Navy ship crew: 16.5 injuries per 100 man-months, overuse musculoskeletal injuries most common.

sources.title: Hearing health risk in a population of aircraft carrier flight deck personnel.
sources.supports: Carrier flight deck crews averaged 109 dBA over 11.5-hour days; 17% of flight deck and 27% of engineers had hearing loss vs 4%.

sources.title: Hospital contacts for noise-related hearing loss among Danish seafarers and fishermen: a population-based cohort study.
sources.supports: Engine room personnel had 2.39 times the hearing loss hospital contacts of other seafarers.

sources.title: The physical and psychological effects of occupational noise among seafarers: a systematic review.
sources.supports: Review: the engine room is the noisiest space aboard; shipboard noise linked to hearing loss and tinnitus.

sources.title: Noise and Military Service: Implications for Hearing Loss and Tinnitus
sources.supports: National Academies review of hazardous military noise and the noise levels that cause hearing loss and tinnitus.
sources.publisher: Institute of Medicine, The National Academies Press

pages.summary: Scuba, surface-supplied and mixed gas diving for salvage, EOD, search and rescue or special operations.

common_conditions.name: Decompression Illness Residuals
common_conditions.reason: Gas bubbles from ascent can damage nerves and bone and leave lasting effects.

common_conditions.name: Eustachian Tube Dysfunction
common_conditions.reason: Pressure changes on descent squeeze the middle ear when ear tubes do not equalize.

common_conditions.name: Sinusitis, pansinusitis, chronic
common_conditions.reason: Sinus squeeze on dives irritates the lining; chronic sinusitis rises with dive count.

common_conditions.name: Tympanic membrane, perforation of
common_conditions.reason: Ear barotrauma can tear the eardrum.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Inner ear barotrauma or inner ear DCS can leave permanent hearing loss.

common_conditions.name: Peripheral vestibular disorders
common_conditions.reason: Inner ear injury from pressure or bubbles can cause lasting balance problems.

common_conditions.name: Chronic otitis externa
common_conditions.reason: Long hours in the water lead to outer ear canal infections in divers.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Heavy dive gear and topside work give Navy divers high rates of back disorders.

sources.title: Long-term neurological sequelae after decompression sickness in retired professional divers.
sources.supports: Retired divers with past decompression sickness had more long-term neurological findings than divers without it.

sources.title: Dysbaric Osteonecrosis in Divers: A Narrative Review With a Systematic Literature Search of Pathophysiology, Prevalence, Clinical Features, and Screening.
sources.supports: Decompression bubbles can kill bone, mostly in the shoulder and hip heads (dysbaric osteonecrosis).

sources.title: Otorhinolaryngologic disorders and diving accidents: an analysis of 306 divers.
sources.supports: 306 divers with ENT problems: Eustachian tube dysfunction most common (24%); chronic sinusitis rose with number of dives.

sources.title: Otitic Barotrauma Due to Eustachian Tube Dysfunction and Special Considerations in At-Risk Populations.
sources.supports: Ear barotrauma, mostly from Eustachian tube dysfunction, is highly prevalent in divers and aircrew; it can injure the eardrum.

sources.title: Diving-related ear, nose, and throat disorders: a structured review using a phase-of-dive framework.
sources.supports: Review: middle ear barotrauma most common; inner ear barotrauma and DCS leave lasting hearing or balance loss; otitis externa.

sources.title: Health conditions among Navy divers at end of service: a retrospective cohort study.
sources.supports: 4,623 separating Navy divers: high rates of joint and back disorders; special warfare divers had high hearing loss rates.

pages.activity_name: Cold weather training and arctic posts
pages.summary: Field training, guard duty or deployment in freezing or wet cold: Alaska, Korea winters, northern Europe, mountains, long hours in wet boots.

common_conditions.name: Cold injury residuals
common_conditions.reason: Frostbite and wet-cold injury damage nerves and blood vessels, leaving pain, numbness and cold sensitivity.

common_conditions.name: Raynaud's Syndrome (Secondary Raynaud's Phenomenon)
common_conditions.reason: Cold injury can damage small blood vessels so fingers and toes turn white and painful in the cold.

common_conditions.name: Degenerative arthritis, other than post-traumatic
common_conditions.reason: Severe cold injury can damage joints and bone in the hands and feet, showing later as arthritis on X-ray.

common_conditions.name: Scar(s), unstable or painful
common_conditions.reason: Frostbite that kills skin can heal with painful or unstable scars on fingers, toes, ears or nose.

common_conditions.name: Malignant skin neoplasms (other than malignant melanoma)
common_conditions.reason: Skin cancer can form years later in old frostbite scars, which VA rates separately from the cold injury.

sources.title: 38 CFR 4.104, Schedule of ratings, cardiovascular system (DC 7122 Cold injury residuals)
sources.supports: Lists cold injury residual findings and says to rate Raynaud's, skin cancer at cold injury scars and amputations separately.

sources.title: Cold Injuries
sources.supports: VA lists long-term cold injury problems: changes in muscle, skin, nails and bones, skin cancer in frostbite scars, nerve injury and Raynaud's.
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Public Health

sources.title: Cold weather injuries among the active and reserve components of the U.S. Armed Forces, July 2019-June 2024.
sources.supports: DoD surveillance of frostbite and other cold injuries each season, with the highest rates in the Army and Marine Corps.

sources.title: Case series of non-freezing cold injury: the modern clinical syndrome.
sources.supports: In 76 service members with non-freezing cold injury, lasting cold sensitivity and abnormal sensation were the main chronic signs.

sources.title: Botulinum Toxin A in the treatment of frostbite sequelae - results from a blinded, early-phase, comparative trial.
sources.supports: Notes freezing cold injuries are associated with long-term sequelae including vasospasm.

pages.summary: Training or deploying in high heat: summer field exercises, ruck marches in heat, desert deployments, work in full gear with little water or shade.

common_conditions.name: Heat Injury Residuals (Heat Stroke / Heat Exhaustion)
common_conditions.reason: Heat stroke can injure the brain, leaving lasting balance, coordination or memory problems in some.

common_conditions.name: Nephrolithiasis/Ureterolithiasis/Nephrocalcinosis
common_conditions.reason: Heavy sweating and too little water concentrate urine, which raises the risk of kidney stones.

common_conditions.name: Chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis
common_conditions.reason: Heat stroke can injure the kidneys; a large cohort found later chronic kidney disease and dialysis more often.

common_conditions.name: Arteriosclerotic heart disease (coronary artery disease)
common_conditions.reason: In a long-term cohort, people who had heat stroke later had more heart attacks than those who had not.

common_conditions.name: Dermatophytosis / Ringworm (Tinea Pedis, Cruris, Capitis, Corporis)
common_conditions.reason: Hot, humid conditions and sweaty boots help fungus grow, so athlete's foot is common in troops.

sources.title: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke among U.S. active component service members, 2021-2025.
sources.supports: DoD surveillance: heat stroke and heat exhaustion rates highest in Marine Corps, Army and recruit training.

sources.title: Review article: Environmental heatstroke and long-term clinical neurological outcomes: A literature review of case reports and case series 2000-2016.
sources.supports: Permanent neurological deficits, mostly cerebellar, were found in about a third of heatstroke survivors with known outcome.

sources.title: Renal lithiasis: addressing the risks of austere desert deployments.
sources.supports: Kidney stone cases in Air Force members deployed to desert bases; field hydration advice may not prevent stones.

sources.title: Update: Urinary stones, active component, U.S. Armed Forces, 2011-2015.
sources.supports: Tracks urinary stones in service members and advises avoiding dehydration to prevent them.

sources.title: Risk of chronic kidney disease in patients with heat injury: A nationwide longitudinal cohort study in Taiwan.
sources.supports: Heat injury patients had about 4 times the risk of chronic kidney disease and 9 times the risk of end-stage renal disease.

sources.title: The association between heat stroke and subsequent cardiovascular diseases.
sources.supports: Over 14 years, heat stroke patients had more heart attacks, strokes and chronic kidney disease than controls.

sources.title: Prevalence of Tinea pedis in military personnel: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.supports: Pooled tinea pedis prevalence of 17% in military personnel, highest in hot and humid regions.

pages.summary: Working on trucks, tanks and tactical vehicles: under-vehicle work, brake jobs, impact wrenches, fuels, oils, solvents and running engines in the bay.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Bending under hoods and lying under vehicles in awkward positions strains the low back.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Working overhead and craning to see into engine bays strains the neck.

common_conditions.name: Dermatitis or eczema
common_conditions.reason: Daily skin contact with oils, fuels and solvents irritates skin and causes hand dermatitis.

common_conditions.name: Raynaud's Syndrome (Secondary Raynaud's Phenomenon)
common_conditions.reason: Years on impact wrenches and air tools can damage finger blood vessels: vibration white finger.

common_conditions.name: Neuritis of median nerve
common_conditions.reason: Forceful, repetitive gripping and vibrating tools raise the risk of carpal tunnel syndrome.

sources.title: Epidemiological study of work-related musculoskeletal disorders and related risk factors among automobile maintenance workers.
sources.supports: In 539 auto maintenance workers, the low back, neck and shoulders were most affected, tied to uncomfortable postures.

sources.title: Assessment of hand or foot eczema and contact dermatitis among car mechanics.
sources.supports: Mineral oil and petroleum contact causes dermatitis in vehicle repair workers; hands most often affected.
sources.publisher: European Review for Medical and Pharmacological Sciences

sources.title: Hand-arm vibration and the risk of vascular and neurological diseases-A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.supports: Vibrating tool users had higher risk of Raynaud's phenomenon (OR 6.9), nerve injury (7.4) and carpal tunnel syndrome (2.9).

sources.title: Work-relatedness of carpal tunnel syndrome: Systematic review including meta-analysis and GRADE.
sources.supports: High-certainty evidence that high hand force and repetition raise carpal tunnel syndrome rates.

pages.summary: Riding up in the turret of a Humvee, MRAP or gun truck on patrols and convoys, behind a .50 cal, M240 or Mk19, with your upper body above the roof.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: Gunfire from the turret and blasts near the truck damage the inner ear; combat jobs show more tinnitus.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Hours of vehicle noise plus weapon fire next to your head wear down hearing over a deployment.

common_conditions.name: Cervical strain (neck)
common_conditions.reason: Out of the hatch, every jolt and swerve whips your neck; military vehicle rides raise neck problems.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Long weeks in tactical vehicles while wearing armor predicted low back pain in a deployed brigade.

common_conditions.name: Residuals of traumatic brain injury (TBI)
common_conditions.reason: Gunners had the highest injury risk of any seat in Humvee crashes, and blast-exposed jobs show more TBI.

common_conditions.name: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
common_conditions.reason: Concussions on deployment, often from blasts, are strongly tied to PTSD afterward.

sources.title: Incidence and Risk Factors for Tinnitus Among Military Service Members in the Millennium Cohort Study
sources.supports: Millennium Cohort: new tinnitus tied to Army or Marine service, combat deployment, combat jobs and mild TBI.

sources.title: Occupational Risk of Low-Level Blast Exposure and TBI-Related Medical Diagnoses: A Population-Based Epidemiological Investigation (2005-2015)
sources.supports: Over 2 million service members: jobs with low-level blast exposure had more TBI, hearing problems, headaches and anxiety.
sources.publisher: International journal of environmental research and public health

sources.title: In-vehicle noise exposure among military personnel depending on type of vehicle, riding compartment and road surface
sources.supports: Noise in military truck cabs and rear compartments exceeded limits, putting riders at high risk of noise hearing loss.

sources.title: Effects of vehicle-ride exposure on cervical pathology: a meta-analysis
sources.supports: Meta-analysis: riding in ground military vehicles raised the odds of neck (cervical) problems (OR 2.33).

sources.title: Injuries to deployed U.S. Army soldiers involved in HMMWV crashes, 2002-2006
sources.supports: Army HMMWV crash data 1999-2006: gunners had the highest injury risk of any seat (OR 2.37), and combat raised risk.

sources.title: Loads worn by soldiers predict episodes of low back pain during deployment to Afghanistan
sources.supports: Deployed Army brigade in Afghanistan: 21 to 40 hours a week in a tactical vehicle and armor time predicted low back pain.

sources.title: Mild traumatic brain injury in U.S. Soldiers returning from Iraq
sources.supports: 2,525 infantry soldiers after Iraq: 43.9% of those knocked out by a concussion met PTSD criteria, vs 9.1% uninjured.
sources.publisher: The New England journal of medicine

pages.activity_name: CS gas chamber and mask confidence training
pages.summary: Breaking the mask seal or pulling it off in a CS-filled chamber in training, or running the chamber as CBRN cadre class after class.

common_conditions.name: Asthma, bronchial
common_conditions.reason: Heavy CS in a closed room can trigger lasting airway twitchiness that acts like asthma.

common_conditions.name: Bronchitis, chronic
common_conditions.reason: CS inflames the airways; chamber trainees get more respiratory illness after exposure.

common_conditions.name: Keratopathy
common_conditions.reason: Tear gas can burn the cornea and, with heavy exposure, leave opacities or nerve damage.

common_conditions.name: Chronic conjunctivitis (nontrachomatous)
common_conditions.reason: CS irritates the eye surface; reviews report lasting conjunctival damage after heavy exposure.

common_conditions.name: Dermatitis or eczema
common_conditions.reason: CS reacts with sweaty skin; some people become sensitized and develop lasting rashes.

sources.title: O-chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS riot control agent) associated acute respiratory illnesses in a U.S. Army Basic Combat Training cohort.
sources.supports: 6,723 Fort Jackson recruits: risk of acute respiratory illness rose 2.44 times after the CS mask confidence chamber.

sources.title: O-chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS riot control agent) exposure in a U.S. Army basic combat training cohort.
sources.supports: Nearly all trainees, and every chamber operator, were exposed to CS above the NIOSH immediately dangerous level.

sources.title: Exposure to the riot control agent CS and potential health effects: a systematic review of the evidence.
sources.supports: Review of 35 studies: skin, eye and breathing effects, with lasting effects tied to enclosed-space exposure.
sources.publisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

sources.title: Reactive airways dysfunction after exposure to teargas.
sources.supports: Case report of reactive airways dysfunction syndrome, an asthma-like condition, after tear gas exposure.

sources.title: Medical hazards of the tear gas CS. A case of persistent, multisystem, hypersensitivity reaction and review of the literature.
sources.supports: CS caused months of dermatitis and asthma-like airway disease still present a year later in a sensitized man.

sources.title: Noxious effects of riot control agents on the ocular surface: Pathogenic mechanisms and management.
sources.supports: Tear gases and pepper spray can cause corneal opacities, neurotrophic keratopathy and conjunctival damage.

sources.title: Extensive Exposure to Tear Gases in Ankara.
sources.supports: Indoor tear gas exposure brought cough, phlegm and lower lung function than outdoor exposure.

pages.activity_name: Main engine rooms and gas turbines
pages.summary: Watches and repairs in main machinery rooms on gas turbine and diesel ships: engines, generators, reduction gears, fuel and lube oil.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Engine room crews have more noise hearing loss than other sailors.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: The engine room is the noisiest space aboard, and that noise is tied to tinnitus.

common_conditions.name: Respiratory System Cancer (Malignant)
common_conditions.reason: Engine room crews had higher lung cancer rates, from exhaust, oil mist and old asbestos.

common_conditions.name: Dermatitis or eczema
common_conditions.reason: Daily skin contact with fuel and lube oil causes hand dermatitis.

common_conditions.name: Chronic Sleep Disturbance
common_conditions.reason: Rotating engineering watches break up sleep and build sleep debt that can become insomnia.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Bending over machinery and climbing ladders in tight spaces strains the low back.

sources.title: Hospital contacts for noise-related hearing loss among Danish seafarers and fishermen: a population-based cohort study.
sources.supports: Civilian seafarers, same engine room work: engine room personnel had 2.39 times the hearing loss hospital contacts of other seafarers.

sources.title: Statistical analysis of hearing loss among navy personnel.
sources.supports: 268,000 enlisted sailors: half a career on surface warships raised the chance of leaving with hearing loss by 13 points.

sources.title: Physical influences on seafarers are different during their voyage episodes of port stay, river passage and sea passage: A maritime field study.
sources.supports: Civilian merchant crews, same spaces: ship field study: engine room 104 dB(A); engine crews averaged 96 dB(A), deck crews 83 dB(A) during work.

sources.title: The physical and psychological effects of occupational noise among seafarers: a systematic review.
sources.supports: Civilian seafarers, same ship noise: review: the engine room is the noisiest space aboard; shipboard noise linked to hearing loss and tinnitus.

sources.title: Occupational noise exposure: A review of its effects, epidemiology, and impact with recommendations for reducing its burden.
sources.supports: Workers in many trades: repeated noise at or above 85 dBA causes permanent hearing loss and tinnitus.

sources.title: Cancer incidence among Danish seafarers: a population based cohort study.
sources.supports: Civilian seafarers, same engine and deck work: danish seafarers: lung cancer risk 2.3 times expected in engine room crew and 4.1 in maintenance crew (exhaust, oil, asbestos).

sources.title: Cancer at sea: a case-control study among male Finnish seafarers.
sources.supports: Civilian seafarers, same engine and deck work: finnish seafarers: engine crew lung cancer rose with years at sea, mesothelioma OR 9.75; icebreaker deck crew had more lung cancer.

sources.title: Assessment of hand or foot eczema and contact dermatitis among car mechanics.
sources.supports: Civilian mechanics, same oils and fuels: mineral oil and petroleum contact causes hand dermatitis in vehicle repair workers.

sources.title: Operational assessment of the 5-h on/10-h off watchstanding schedule on a US Navy ship: sleep patterns, mood and psychomotor vigilance performance of crewmembers in the nuclear reactor department.
sources.supports: Sailors on a rotating 5/10 watch built up sleep debt from long workdays and sleep out of sync with the body clock.

sources.title: Sleep in the United States Military.
sources.supports: Review: night shifts and continuous ops cause insufficient sleep, tied to insomnia, sleep apnea, PTSD and heart disease.

sources.title: Epidemiological study of work-related musculoskeletal disorders and related risk factors among automobile maintenance workers.
sources.supports: Civilian mechanics, same postures: in 539 auto maintenance workers, the low back, neck and shoulders were most affected, tied to awkward postures.

sources.title: Incidence and Mechanisms of Musculoskeletal Injuries in Deployed Navy Active Duty Service Members Aboard Two U.S. Navy Air Craft Carriers.
sources.supports: On two deployed carriers, low back (34%), shoulder (25%) and knee (15%) were the most common musculoskeletal complaints.

pages.summary: Arc, MIG and TIG welding, torch cutting and grinding on vehicles, equipment and structures, often in tight spaces full of fumes and noise.

common_conditions.name: Respiratory System Cancer (Malignant)
common_conditions.reason: Welding fumes are a known lung carcinogen, even after accounting for smoking and asbestos.

common_conditions.name: Asthma, bronchial
common_conditions.reason: Welders develop adult-onset asthma more often; nickel in the fume is one driver.

common_conditions.name: Bronchitis, chronic
common_conditions.reason: Years of fume and dust raise the risk of chronic bronchitis in welders.

common_conditions.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
common_conditions.reason: Dust and chromium in weld fume were tied to COPD in a welder cohort.

common_conditions.name: Allergic or vasomotor rhinitis
common_conditions.reason: Welders show higher rates of new rhinitis from breathing metal fume.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Grinding, cutting and metal shop noise wears down hearing over years of work.

common_conditions.name: Tinnitus, recurrent
common_conditions.reason: The same metal shop noise can leave lasting ringing in the ears.

common_conditions.name: Arm, limitation of motion of
common_conditions.reason: Holding a torch or grinder with arms raised for long periods is linked to shoulder impingement.

common_conditions.name: Unhealed eye injury
common_conditions.reason: Grinding throws metal slivers into the eye that often heal with a corneal scar.

sources.title: Welding fumes and lung cancer: a meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies.
sources.supports: IARC-led meta-analysis: welding fumes raise lung cancer risk regardless of steel type, after adjusting for smoking and asbestos (civilian welders, same task).

sources.title: Incidence of rhinitis and asthma related to welding in Northern Europe.
sources.supports: Population study in Northern Europe: welders had higher incidence of adult-onset rhinitis and, in men, asthma (civilian welders, same task).

sources.title: Respiratory Ill-Health and Welding Exposures: A Canadian Cohort Study.
sources.supports: Canadian welder cohort: welders had more asthma, rhinitis and COPD/bronchitis, tied to dust, chromium and nickel in fume (civilian welders, same task).

sources.title: Noise-induced hearing loss in small-scale metal industry in Nepal.
sources.supports: Metal workers had far more noise-induced hearing loss than unexposed controls (civilian metal shops, same task).
sources.publisher: The Journal of laryngology and otology

sources.title: Occupational noise exposure: A review of its effects, epidemiology, and impact with recommendations for reducing its burden.
sources.supports: Review: repeated noise at or above 85 dBA causes permanent hearing loss and tinnitus; construction and mining have the highest burden (civilian workers, same task).
sources.publisher: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

sources.title: Noise Exposure
sources.supports: VA: noise from machinery, heavy weapons and aircraft in general job duties can cause or contribute to hearing loss and tinnitus.
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Public Health

sources.title: Associations between work-related factors and specific disorders of the shoulder--a systematic review of the literature.
sources.supports: Systematic review: working with arms raised, forceful exertion and repetitive work are linked to shoulder impingement (civilian workers, same task).
sources.publisher: Scandinavian journal of work, environment & health

sources.title: Corneal metallic foreign body injuries due to suboptimal ocular protection.
sources.supports: Hospital series: most metallic corneal foreign bodies came from grinding and 88% healed with a corneal scar (civilian workers, same task).

pages.summary: Base and shipboard fire crews: structure fires, smoke, SCBA, ladders and hose lines, sirens, 24-hour shifts, and rescues on crash and medical calls.

common_conditions.name: Malignant neoplasms of the genitourinary system
common_conditions.reason: Smoke and soot carcinogens raise bladder cancer risk in firefighters; prostate and testis also rise.

common_conditions.name: Respiratory System Cancer (Malignant)
common_conditions.reason: Firefighting causes mesothelioma, a cancer of the lining around the lungs, per IARC.

common_conditions.name: Malignant neoplasms of the digestive system, exclusive of skin growths
common_conditions.reason: Career firefighters show higher colon cancer rates in pooled cohort studies.

common_conditions.name: Malignant melanoma
common_conditions.reason: Firefighters have a higher rate of skin melanoma in pooled cohort studies.

common_conditions.name: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
common_conditions.reason: Firefighting is linked to a modest rise in non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

common_conditions.name: Neoplasm, malignant, any specified part of the endocrine system
common_conditions.reason: Pooled firefighter studies found more thyroid cancer than expected.

common_conditions.name: Hearing loss, bilateral sensorineural
common_conditions.reason: Sirens, pumps, saws and alarms are loud; nearly 30% of tested firefighters had hearing loss.

common_conditions.name: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
common_conditions.reason: Burn victims, dead children and injured crew members add up; event load tracks PTSD symptoms.

common_conditions.name: Arteriosclerotic heart disease (coronary artery disease)
common_conditions.reason: Heavy exertion in hot gear strains the heart; coronary disease causes most on-duty firefighter cardiac deaths.

common_conditions.name: Hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension)
common_conditions.reason: About 4 in 10 firefighters have high blood pressure in pooled studies.

common_conditions.name: Sleep Apnea Syndromes (Obstructive, Central, Mixed)
common_conditions.reason: Broken sleep on 24-hour shifts; 28% of firefighters screened positive for sleep apnea.

common_conditions.name: Lumbosacral strain (low back)
common_conditions.reason: Hauling hose, ladders and victims in heavy gear makes the low back the most common pain site.

sources.title: Volume 132: Occupational exposure as a firefighter
sources.supports: IARC Group 1: firefighting causes mesothelioma and bladder cancer; limited evidence for colon, prostate, testis, melanoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (civilian firefighters, same task).
sources.publisher: International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC Monographs)

sources.title: Firefighting and Cancer: A Meta-analysis of Cohort Studies in the Context of Cancer Hazard Identification.
sources.supports: IARC meta-analysis: career firefighters had higher rates of mesothelioma, bladder, prostate, testicular, colon, thyroid cancer, melanoma and NHL (civilian firefighters, same task).

sources.title: Prevalence of Hearing Loss and Perceptions of Hearing Health and Protection among Florida Firefighters.
sources.supports: Nearly 30% of 214 audiometry-tested firefighters had mild to profound hearing loss, worse than aging alone (civilian firefighters, same task).
sources.publisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

sources.title: Duty-related trauma and PTSD symptoms in US urban firefighters.
sources.supports: 755 career firefighters: event load and the stress of duty-related events were linked to PTSD symptoms (civilian firefighters, same task).

sources.title: Rescuers at risk: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis of the worldwide current prevalence and correlates of PTSD in rescue workers.
sources.supports: 28 studies, 20,424 rescue workers including firefighters: pooled PTSD prevalence of 10%, much higher than the general population.

sources.title: Sudden Cardiac Death in Firefighters From the United States: A 16-Year Postmortem Analysis.
sources.supports: 39.3% of autopsied on-duty firefighter deaths were sudden cardiac death; 81.8% were due to coronary or hypertensive heart disease (civilian firefighters, same task).
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Heart Association

sources.title: The Prevalence of Metabolic Syndrome and Its Components in Firefighters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.supports: 25 studies, 31,309 firefighters: hypertension prevalence 39.1% (civilian firefighters, same task).
sources.publisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

sources.title: Common sleep disorders increase risk of motor vehicle crashes and adverse health outcomes in firefighters.
sources.supports: 6,933 firefighters: 28.4% screened positive for obstructive sleep apnea; sleep disorders tied to crashes, heart disease, depression (civilian firefighters, same task).

sources.title: The global prevalence of musculoskeletal disorders among firefighters: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.supports: 31 studies: 41% of firefighters had musculoskeletal disorders; low back the most common site at 31% (civilian firefighters, same task).
sources.publisher: International Journal of Occupational Safety and Ergonomics

pages.summary: Desert Shield and Desert Storm: months in Saudi and Kuwaiti desert, the ground push, PB pills, bug spray, smoke and tent life.

common_conditions.name: Chronic Multi-Symptom Illness (Gulf War Illness)
common_conditions.reason: Fatigue, pain and memory trouble with no clear cause are covered for Gulf War vets under 38 CFR 3.317.

common_conditions.name: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS)
common_conditions.reason: Gulf War vets had nearly 5 times the CFS-like illness; 38 CFR 3.317 covers chronic fatigue syndrome.

common_conditions.name: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
common_conditions.reason: IBS is common in Gulf War vets and counts as a functional GI disorder under 38 CFR 3.317.

common_conditions.name: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
common_conditions.reason: Gulf War vets had about 3 times the PTSD of era peers, rising with deployment stress.

common_conditions.name: Fibromyalgia (fibrositis, primary fibromyalgia syndrome)
common_conditions.reason: Widespread muscle pain with no clear cause, fibromyalgia, is covered under 38 CFR 3.317.

common_conditions.name: Asthma, bronchial
common_conditions.reason: VA presumes asthma after Gulf War service under 38 CFR 3.320; dust and smoke inflame airways.

common_conditions.name: Allergic or vasomotor rhinitis
common_conditions.reason: VA presumes rhinitis after Gulf War service under 38 CFR 3.320; particles irritate the nose.

common_conditions.name: Sinusitis, pansinusitis, chronic
common_conditions.reason: VA presumes sinusitis after Gulf War service under 38 CFR 3.320; particles block sinus drainage.

sources.title: 38 CFR 3.317, Compensation for certain disabilities occurring in Persian Gulf veterans
sources.supports: Covers undiagnosed illness and chronic multisymptom illness (CFS, fibromyalgia, functional GI disorders like IBS) and nine infectious diseases for Southwest Asia and Afghanistan.

sources.title: Chronic multisymptom illness affecting Air Force veterans of the Gulf War.
sources.supports: Chronic multisymptom illness hit 45% of 1,155 Air Force Gulf War veterans vs 15% of nondeployed peers.

sources.title: Health of US veterans of 1991 Gulf War: a follow-up survey in 10 years.
sources.supports: Fourteen years later, Gulf War vets still reported more multisymptom illness, CFS-like illness, PTSD and other conditions than era controls.

sources.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder and chronic fatigue syndrome-like illness among Gulf War veterans: a population-based survey of 30,000 veterans.
sources.supports: Survey of 30,000 veterans: Gulf War vets had 3 times the PTSD and nearly 5 times the CFS-like illness of era peers; PTSD rose with deployment stress.

sources.title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome in Veterans With Gulf War Illness Evaluated at VA's War-Related Illness and Injury Study Center.
sources.supports: Among 578 deployed Gulf War vets seen at the WRIISC, half had physician-diagnosed IBS, tied to severe Gulf War illness.

sources.title: Gulf War Illnesses linked to Southwest Asia service
sources.supports: Undiagnosed illnesses (CFS, fibromyalgia, functional GI disorders) and infectious diseases VA connects to Gulf War service from 1990 to now.

sources.title: 38 CFR 3.320, Claims based on exposure to fine particulate matter
sources.supports: Presumes asthma, rhinitis and sinusitis (and rare airway cancers) for Southwest Asia theater service, and Afghanistan, Syria, Djibouti or Uzbekistan after Sept. 19, 2001.
sources.publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office (Code of Federal Regulations)

pages.activity_name: Living on bases with burn pits
pages.summary: Living, working or pulling details near open burn pits on bases in Iraq, Afghanistan and nearby countries after 9/11.

common_conditions.reason: More days at burn pit bases raised asthma odds; VA presumes asthma here under 38 CFR 3.320.

common_conditions.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
common_conditions.reason: Each 100 days at a burn pit base raised COPD odds; VA lists COPD under the PACT Act.

common_conditions.name: Allergic or vasomotor rhinitis
common_conditions.reason: Smoke and dust irritate the nose; VA presumes rhinitis for this service under 38 CFR 3.320.

common_conditions.name: Sinusitis, pansinusitis, chronic
common_conditions.reason: VA presumes sinusitis for this service under 38 CFR 3.320; rhinosinusitis began on deployment.

common_conditions.name: Hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension)

common_conditions.name: Bronchitis, chronic
common_conditions.reason: Smoke inflames the bronchial tubes; VA lists chronic bronchitis for burn pit locations.

common_conditions.name: Diffuse interstitial fibrosis (interstitial pneumonitis, fibrosing alveolitis)
common_conditions.reason: VA lists interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis for burn pit service under the PACT Act.

common_conditions.name: Sarcoidosis
common_conditions.reason: VA lists sarcoidosis and granulomatous disease for burn pit service under the PACT Act.

common_conditions.name: Emphysema, pulmonary

common_conditions.name: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
common_conditions.reason: VA lists lymphoma of any type for burn pit locations under the PACT Act.

common_conditions.reason: VA lists brain cancer and glioblastoma for burn pit locations under the PACT Act.

sources.title: Deployment to Military Bases With Open Burn Pits and Respiratory and Cardiovascular Disease.

sources.title: New-Onset Asthma and Combat Deployment: Findings From the Millennium Cohort Study.

sources.title: 38 CFR 3.320, Claims based on exposure to fine particulate matter
sources.supports: Presumes asthma, rhinitis and sinusitis (and rare airway cancers) for Southwest Asia theater service, and Afghanistan, Syria, Djibouti or Uzbekistan after Sept. 19, 2001.

sources.title: Exposure to burn pits and other specific environmental hazards
sources.supports: Names the Mishraq sulfur fire and Qarmat Ali hexavalent chromium exposures, and lists burn pit cancers and lung illnesses VA treats as presumptive under the PACT Act.

sources.title: Sinusitis and rhinitis among US veterans deployed to Southwest Asia and Afghanistan after September 11, 2001.
sources.supports: VA SHADE study of 1,960 post-9/11 land deployers: rhinitis and sinusitis began during and after deployment; rhinitis tied to pesticide and repellent use.

sources.title: Deployment-related respiratory health: bridging the gap between clinical and epidemiological associations and disease mechanisms: an official American Thoracic Society Workshop Report.
sources.supports: ATS workshop: land deployers to Southwest Asia and Afghanistan breathed high particulate levels from desert dust, burn pits and jobs, with lung effects.

pages.summary: Serving aboard ships within 12 nautical miles of Vietnam or Cambodia between 1962 and 1975, including gunline, Yankee Station and offshore duty.

common_conditions.name: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
common_conditions.reason: VA presumes non-Hodgkin's lymphoma after herbicide exposure under 38 CFR 3.309(e).

common_conditions.name: AL amyloidosis (primary amyloidosis)

sources.title: Health status of Army Chemical Corps Vietnam veterans who sprayed defoliant in Vietnam.

sources.title: Agent Orange exposure and disability compensation

sources.title: Herbicide Exposure, Vietnam Service, and Hypertension Risk in Army Chemical Corps Veterans.

sources.title: Blue Water Navy Veterans and Agent Orange Exposure
sources.supports: Public Law 116-23 extended the herbicide exposure presumption to ships within 12 nautical miles of Vietnam and Cambodia, 1962 to 1975.

common_conditions.name: Malignant neoplasms of the genitourinary system
